Question: Would it possible for me to rig this house to mount on a 4x4 wood post? Like screwed through the bottom onto and wood base plate or something?
Answer: I wouldn't suggest it as the pole is an integral part of the house's support structure. There's a molded-in bracket on the bottom of the house and a channel up thru the center of the house that the pole fits into which helps add rigidity to the structure. The amount of work you'd do trying to jury-rig another support system and the possibility of fracturing the plastic base through screws torquing the house in ways it wasn't designed to be twisted might prove expensive in the short run. Once you erect the house on the pole and see how it reacts in the wind I believe you'll see the reason to build it as it was designed. I'd use Froogle.com or another shop-bot to find the S&K pole and ground socket at a good price and use it. I have four BN-16s up now, all bought off-season and on sale. I find it an easy house to maintain. I mounted the ground sleeve the pole slides into in cement - I used a 12" wide piece of heavy duty paper construction tube cut to the same size as the sleeve and set it slightly below ground level so that, with the pole removed, I can mow over the area. I mixed the cement in an old plastic tub, used the bottom portion of the aluminum mounting tube with a level to make sure the sleeve was vertical - a little elbow grease but no major task. The house seems fragile but when combined with the pole it's designed to work with my houses rode out Hurricane Issac last year with no damage OR loss of the few birds that hadn't left yet.

Question: DSLR with Image stabilization in camera body or the lens ?? which is better: So is it better to buy camera body with IS and save some money with lenses as camera already has IS or invest more for lenses with IS??
Answer: Ah Grasshopper, As in most things in life, the answer depends on who you ask (says the old Kung-Fu matser as he strokes his long, white beard) The argument in favor of in-body image stabilization sounds very convincing on the surface: Pay for the extra cost just once, save on all existing lenses, or new lenses that follow. If you already have some good lenses from Pentax, Olympus or Minolta, then choosing a corresponding dSLR body with built-in image stabilization makes perfect sense. If not, then consider the following counter-arguments: 1. Good lenses (with or without IS) are often more expensive than a digital camera body, and have longer lifespan. Your digital camera body will most likely be obsolete in 4-5 years, but good lenses may serve you for 10 years or longer. So it makes less sense to pay extra for dSLR body with built-in IS. 2. Image stabilization is needed most at longer focus length, but in-body IS (mechanical moving the sensor) is only effective at shorter focus length. Let's assume that the sensor can travel up to 1mm in any direction. When focus length=50mm, this 1mm travel corresponse to 1.1 degree of angular rotation (correction for camera shake). But to achieve the same 1.1 degree correction at 300mm, the sensor needs to travel by 6mm! Even if this kind of travel were possible, the inertia of sensor unit will make the response very slow. With optical IS this is not a problem - because light has no inertia. 3. Optical IS gives you a stable image when you look through the optical view finder, so you know exectly how well it is working. Mechanical IS cannot give you a stable image through the optical view finder.

Question: Will this Fobus paddle holster fit a Beretta Nano .9mm pistol securely?
Answer: Not even close. This particular holster is designed for the Beretta 92 series style pistols (and Taurus clones) which are full frame duty size pistols, much like the standard issue sidearm carried by United States Armed Forces in combat, the Beretta M9. The Nano is a tiny pocket pistol that is dwarfed in size by the pistols that this holster is intended for. To my knowledge, there aren't any cheep outside the waistband (OWB) style holsters that would fit the Beretta Nano. It is a pistol designed for deep concealment or pocket carry and there isn't much demand for a plastic or kydex OWB holster. Also, I assume that you are new to firearms and made a simple mistake. There is no such thing as a ".9mm" caliber. The period is actually a decimal point and is only to be used with calibers that are measured in inches. For example, a .45 ACP is roughly .45 inches in diameter. A .44 Magnum is roughly .44 inches in diameter. By virtue of "mm" after the number, a 9mm bullet's diameter is measured in millimeters. If expressed in inches, a 9mm bullet would be about .355 inches in diameter, or .355 caliber. A .9 millimeter bullet, if it existed, would be barely the width of a needle.

The medium in the heat pad is a super cooled solution (sodium acetate and water), that has been cooled below it's freezing point (roughly 130 F/54 C), but remains in a liquid state. Flexing the disk causes nucleation points for a crystallization process. This generates heat up to freezing point of the solution (130 F/54 C) as the crystals form. Question: How much power is supplied to each USB port, and overall?

Since the power supply is only 4A at 5V, you're only going to be able to power four USB 3.0 devices (900mA x 4 = 3.6A) OR eight USB 2.0 devices (500mA x 8 = 4A). Perhaps Manhattan should do what Anker does and use a 12V adapter and whatever they do to undervolt/cut down their USB 3.0 9-port hub to 5V per port (that thing comes with a 12V, 5A power adapter! The brick is almost as big as most laptop power bricks!) Using the formula of Volts x Amps = Watts (5V x 15.6A = 78W), we can conclude that at 12V, only 6.5A would be needed (12V x 6.5A = 78W). Otherwise, they are functionally the same, to anybody except the fine-tuners on the AVS forum board who say they can tell (and yet split as to their preference). I think, at least as to last year's models, that Consumer Reports placed the Samsung slightly above the Panny Viera, while the Cnet reviewer did the opposite. So my opinion is that both are great. I admit though that at home (as opposed to Big Box stores) I have only seen the sammys, and I know they are great.
